newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavarian abortion law blocked by top German court.
newsitem.headline: Bavarian abortion law blocked by top German court.

text.p: Germany's highest court on Tuesday blocked a move by the southern state of Bavaria to introduce restrictions on abortion tougher than those laid down in national law.
Judges at the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe said key parts of Bavaria's law on abortion should not be implemented until the high court completed a full examination of their implications.
Opponents of the law hailed the court's decision as a victory for women's right to choose and urged Bavaria's ruling conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) to withdraw the plan.

The measures, due to come into force in the strongly Roman Catholic state on July 1, stipulated that doctors could earn no more than a quarter of their incomes from abortions and placed tough conditions on which doctors could carry out terminations.

"The Bavarian government didn't just want to punish the doctors. Its laws were targeted above all at women who decide to have an abortion," said Rita Griesshaber, Greens party's spokeswoman on women's affairs.

Bavaria's Social Affairs Minister Barbara Stamm vowed the state would fight on with its plans and said she was confident the court would have no objections to the measures once it had studied them in detail.

Germany's current national abortion law, approved by parliament in 1995, was a painstaking compromise between the conservative policy of West Germany and the far more liberal abortion-on-demand practised in communist East Germany.

Under the law, abortion is permitted in the first three months of pregnancy if a woman first seeks counselling. But Bavaria felt the law still did not do enough to protect the rights of the unborn child.

In addition to placing restrictions on doctors' income from abortion, its legislation also seeks to limit the number of doctors permitted to carry out terminations by authorising only gynaecologists with a special licence.
"The Bavarian law aimed to have doctors performing as few abortions as possible," said Uta Meier, the head of Profamilia, a lobby group which defends women's right to choose abortion.
"Women from Bavaria would be forced to travel to other regions or to go abroad for a termination."

The court said only 14 gynaecologists had applied for the special licences at the moment when it came to make its decision, meaning Bavaria could not fulfil a legal obligation to provide local health care for women considering an abortion.
But Stamm said this should not be a problem when the court came to its final verdict as 56 doctors had now applied.
A final decision is not expected before the end of the year.
